widgets_values: This is just one example, but when creating a long video by stitching clips together, it’s best to set up a separate workflow like the one shown below.

My process is actually quite simple: I create a series of short clips by ensuring consistency between the starting and ending frames. I always specify an 'end image' for every clip and then stitch them all together at the end. Achieving this consistency might seem difficult, but with the right techniques, it’s manageable.

To achieve consistent image generation, an inpainting workflow is a must.

I’m a huge fan of the workflows by UmeAiRT and PotatCat and use them constantly. 
https://civitai.com/articles/21346
https://civitai.com/articles/9971

I couldn't have made these videos without their amazing contributions to the community.

Please check their webpage for instructions on how to use the Inpaint workflow. Note that I do not use UmeAiRT’s upscale option. PotatCat’s workflow is unique because it enlarges the masked area for the model to regenerate, which helps preserve fine details.

One of the key settings in the Inpaint workflow is the Denoise strength. Generally, it’s best to work with a Denoise value around 0.6. While increasing it toward 1.0 makes the masked area follow your prompts more closely, it often sacrifices the overall consistency of the image. Therefore, I usually establish the rough composition first, then apply inpainting at around 0.6 to refine the details. You can also use the ComfyUI mask editor to lay down basic colors or use external apps like Photoshop to create a rough layout before refining it with 0.6 Denoise inpainting.

A common issue when creating videos with FLF2V—especially when using the same image for both start and end frames—is a sudden color shift that makes the loop seam noticeable. In such cases, I recommend slightly modifying the end image using the Inpaint workflow. Instead of tedious tasks like redrawing outlines, try regenerating just the surfaces—such as skin texture, hair, or clothing wrinkles—at 0.6 Denoise. These subtle changes to the start and end images guide the video model to express motion more naturally and eliminate color inconsistencies.

Additionally, you can create a dynamic camera view simply by cropping the end image while maintaining the original aspect ratio.

Since an end image is already specified, the character's movement remains stable even when you give bold or dramatic commands. In fact, prompting for two or more actions within a 5-second clip will make the movement feel much more dynamic.

When creating your end image, however, be sure to keep the actions within what can realistically happen in under 5 seconds.

Also, if something needs to appear from off-screen, you must include it in the end image. If the video model is forced to generate something that wasn't there to begin with, it often leads to unintended or glitched results.

If you want to extend the video, enter a 16fps WebP format image here.
Then connect it to the Previous Video of the PainterLongVideo node.
At this time, disconnect the start image.
If you do not use Sage Attention, bypass Patch Sage Attention KJ.
If you use negative prompts, bypass ConditioningZeroOut.

WebP 16fps is used when extending a video.
WebP 32fps is used when splicing together the final finished video.
Saving in WebP format takes a while, so it's best to bypass it normally and save it in WebP format once you've output a video you like.

This group was used to embed metadata in videos.
It is not normally used, so please bypass it.
Also, when stitching videos together, use Image Batch Extend With Overlap, and it is recommended that the overlap value be in the range of 1-5.
You can also use the Merge Images node.

Please use whichever frame interpolation you prefer.
⚡ Rife Tensorrt is fast.
